text: Nobody knows for sure, but the best guess is a long-necked plant-eater called Argentinosaurus. It lived in what is now [[@argentina|Argentina]] about 95 million years ago. It was perhaps 30–35 m long, about as long as three school buses, and may have weighed 65–80 tonnes. That is as much as a dozen African elephants.

Argentinosaurus was a titanosaur, one of the last and largest groups of [[sauropod|sauropods]]. Several other titanosaurs come close in size. Because the biggest ones are known from only a handful of bones, the title of "biggest dinosaur" could change with the next dig.

st.reveal: The heaviest blue whales weigh around 150 tonnes or more, about twice the best guesses for Argentinosaurus. Water holds up a whale's body. On land, legs have to carry all the weight, which limits how big an animal can get.

sec.t:
In 1987, a rancher named Guillermo Heredia found a huge bone on his land in Neuquén province, in Patagonia. He thought it was a piece of petrified wood. It turned out to be part of a leg bone. Scientists who came to dig found backbones, ribs and pieces of hip.

They named the animal Argentinosaurus in 1993. One backbone from its middle is about 1.6 m tall. Put it beside a ten-year-old and it would look down on them.

That is still not much of an animal. No skull has been found, and almost none of the neck or tail. Every picture and model of Argentinosaurus fills the gaps using its better-known cousins, so the long neck and small head you see in books are educated guesses.

sec.h: How do you weigh a fossil?
sec.t:
You cannot put a dinosaur on a [[@weights-mass|scale]], so scientists use clues. One method uses living animals. Heavier animals need thicker leg bones, so the thickness of the thigh and upper-arm bones gives a rough weight. Another method builds a 3D model of the body around the skeleton and works out its volume.

Both methods give a range, not one number. For Argentinosaurus, which has only a broken leg bone, the guesses are especially wide. This kind of careful [[@estimation|estimation]] is common in science. You give your best figure and say how sure you are.

In 2017, scientists named Patagotitan, another Argentine titanosaur known from several skeletons. Their best estimate for it was around 57–69 tonnes. A cast of it is so long that, at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, its head pokes out into the next room. Another cast stands in the Field Museum in Chicago.

India has a mysterious contender too. In 1989, scientists described Bruhathkayosaurus, meaning "huge-bodied lizard", from rocks in Tamil Nadu. Its leg bones, as described, would make it a rival to Argentinosaurus. But the [[fossil|fossils]] fell apart and were never properly studied again, so most experts do not count it. A giant backbone found in Colorado during the [[@bone-wars|Bone Wars]] of the 1870s had the same fate. It was drawn and measured, and then it disappeared.

sec.h: How did they get so big?
sec.t:
Sauropods had a few tricks that let them grow huge. Their [[@sauropod-necks|long necks]] let them feed over a wide area without walking much. Their bones were full of air spaces, linked to a breathing system like a bird's, which made the skeleton lighter. And they did not chew. They swallowed leaves whole and let their gut do the work.

They also grew very fast. A baby hatched from an [[@dino-eggs|egg]] smaller than a football and may have reached full size in a few decades. Even so, no dinosaur matched [[@ocean-giants|the blue whale]], which still holds the [[@animal-records|record for the heaviest animal]] known.

text: Scientists compare dinosaur bones with their closest living relatives: birds and [[@croc-ancient|crocodiles]].
Bumps on bones show where muscles were. Skin prints and feather [[fossil|fossils]] show the outside. Footprints show how the animal stood and walked.

Good scientists say clearly which parts are evidence and which parts are guesses. A skeleton is usually solid evidence. The colour of the skin, the shape of soft parts and how the animal behaved are much harder to know.

sec.t:
First, the bones must be cleaned, measured and put in the right order. That is harder than it sounds. Skeletons are rarely complete, and bones from different animals can get mixed up in the rock. Missing parts are often filled in from related animals, or from the opposite side of the same body.

[[@joints|Joints]] show how bones fitted and moved, a bit like hinges. Scientists check how far each joint could bend, so they can pose the skeleton in a way the living animal could really have stood. Your own [[@bones|bones]] carry similar clues about how you move.

Muscles attach to bones with tough [[tendon|tendons]], and they leave marks: rough patches, ridges and bumps. By finding these scars on fossil bones, scientists can work out where the big [[@muscles|muscles]] were and roughly how large they were.

Here the living relatives help most. Birds and crocodiles sit on either side of dinosaurs in the family tree. If both have a particular muscle in the same place, dinosaurs very likely had it too. This idea is called the extant phylogenetic bracket. "Extant" just means "still living".

Today, scientists use CT scanners to look inside fossils without breaking them. They can make digital copies, fix crushed bones on a computer and print them in 3D. [[@3d-printing|3D printing]] also lets museums share exact copies of rare fossils.

Computer models can test how an animal moved. Scientists add virtual muscles to a scanned skeleton and see whether it can walk, run or swim. That is how teams argue about questions like whether [[@dino-swim|Spinosaurus swam]].

Skin is the hardest part. A few dinosaurs left skin impressions, and some feathered ones preserved [[@dino-colors|colour clues]]. For most, artists must decide how much fat, skin and feather to add. Many older drawings were "shrink-wrapped", with skin stretched tightly over the bones. Real animals have fat, cheeks and fluffy coats. A shrink-wrapped elephant or [[@birds-dinosaurs|bird]] would look very strange.

That is why modern palaeoartists work closely with scientists, and why dinosaur pictures keep changing as new evidence comes in.

text: Space weather is what happens when the Sun throws energy and particles out into space and some of it reaches Earth. Like weather on Earth, it can be calm or stormy.

The Sun gives off a steady stream of charged particles called the solar wind. Sometimes it also has explosions. A solar flare is a sudden flash of energy. A coronal mass ejection, or CME, is a giant cloud of hot, charged gas, called [[plasma|plasma]], flung into space. When a big CME hits Earth's magnetic field, it causes a geomagnetic storm. Storms like this can make beautiful auroras, but they can also disturb satellites, power lines, radio signals and GPS.

sec.h: Flares and clouds from the Sun
sec.t:
The Sun is a huge ball of plasma, crossed by twisted magnetic fields. Around [[@sunspots|sunspots]], those fields can tangle and suddenly snap into a new shape, releasing energy.

A solar flare's light travels at the speed of light, so it reaches Earth in about 8 minutes. It can disrupt radio signals on the side of Earth facing the Sun. A CME is slower. It can take one to three days to cross the 15 crore km to Earth. That gives forecasters a little time to warn satellite operators and power companies.

On 1 September 1859, the English [[astronomer|astronomer]] Richard Carrington was sketching sunspots when he saw two bright flashes of white light. About 17 hours later, a huge geomagnetic storm hit Earth.

Auroras lit up the sky as far south as the Caribbean. People in some places got up thinking it was dawn. [[@telegraph|Telegraph]] wires sparked, some operators got electric shocks, and some found they could send messages with their batteries unplugged. It remains the strongest geomagnetic storm on record.

In March 1989, a geomagnetic storm caused a blackout across the Canadian province of Quebec. Millions of people lost power for about nine hours.

In February 2022, SpaceX launched 49 new [[@starlink|Starlink]] satellites just before a minor storm. The storm warmed and puffed up the upper atmosphere, increasing drag. Around 38 of the satellites fell back and burned up.

In May 2024, the strongest storm in about two decades brought auroras to places where they're almost never seen. In India, cameras at the Indian Astronomical Observatory in Hanle, [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], recorded a red aurora low on the horizon. People in the southern United States saw them too.

Forecasters keep watch with spacecraft and ground [[observatory|observatories]]. In the US, NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center in Boulder, Colorado, issues alerts and rates storms from G1 (minor) to G5 (extreme).

India launched its own Sun observatory, [[@aditya-l1|Aditya-L1]], in September 2023. It sits about 15 lakh km from Earth, at a point where it can watch the Sun without Earth ever getting in the way. It studies flares, CMEs and the solar wind.

The Sun's activity rises and falls in a cycle of about 11 years. At solar maximum there are more sunspots, flares and storms. NASA and NOAA announced in October 2024 that the Sun had reached the maximum phase of its current cycle. Over the next several years, activity should slowly calm down, before rising again in the 2030s.

Astronauts on the International Space Station have a sheltered area to move to during a strong storm. For the rest of us, a big solar storm mostly means a chance to look up at the right moment.

text: An aircraft carrier's runway is far too short for a normal landing, so carrier planes are built to stop in a hurry. Each one has a strong steel hook, called a tailhook, hanging under its tail. Stretched across the back of the deck are three or four thick steel cables, called arresting wires.

The pilot flies down at a steep, steady angle and slams the plane onto the deck instead of floating down gently. The hook snags one of the wires. Machinery below deck lets the wire pay out under huge resistance, and the plane goes from about 240 km/h to a stop in roughly 100 metres. Pilots call it a "controlled crash".

st.reveal: If the hook misses all the wires, the jet needs enough speed to fly off the end of the deck and come round again. So pilots go to full power on touchdown. If the hook catches, the wire stops the plane anyway.

myth: Planes land on aircraft carriers by braking very hard with their wheels.

Wheel brakes alone would need a runway far longer than any ship. Most carrier jets stop by catching a steel cable with a hook under the tail. The cable is linked to machinery below deck that pays it out and slows the jet smoothly.

sec.t:
On 18 January 1911, an American pilot named Eugene Ely flew a flimsy biplane towards the warship USS Pennsylvania in San Francisco Bay. A wooden platform had been built over the ship's back deck. Ropes stretched across it were tied to bags of sand on each side.

Hooks on Ely's plane caught the ropes, and the sandbags dragged him to a stop. It was the first time a plane had landed on a ship. The idea was simple, and modern carriers still use the same basic trick, with steel cables and hydraulic machinery in place of rope and sand.

Taking off is the opposite problem: getting a heavy jet up to flying speed on a short deck. Big American carriers use catapults, which fling the plane forward, from standstill to over 200 km/h in about two seconds. Older ones use steam, while the newest, USS Gerald R. Ford, uses powerful electric motors.

India's carriers use a ski-jump instead. The front of the deck curves upward, so planes leave the ship angled into the sky. That gives them a few extra seconds to build speed before they need to fly. It helps to know [[@airplanes-fly|how planes fly]]: a wing needs fast-moving air over it to make enough lift.

India has had aircraft carriers since 1961. The first INS Vikrant, bought from Britain, played a part in the [[@1971-war|1971 war]] in the Bay of Bengal. Today the Indian Navy operates INS Vikramaditya, a converted Russian ship, and a new INS Vikrant.

The new Vikrant was designed in India and built at Cochin Shipyard in Kerala. It was commissioned on 2 September 2022. It is about 262 metres long, roughly the length of two and a half football fields, and its pilots are naval aviators, not members of the [[@indian-air-force|Indian Air Force]].

The largest American carriers are over 330 metres long and carry more than 5,000 people, with kitchens, hospitals, gyms and a post office on board. They weigh about 100,000 tonnes and still [[@floating-ships|float]], because their huge hulls push aside a weight of water greater than their own.

Not every aircraft needs the wires. [[@helicopters|Helicopters]] can land almost anywhere on the deck, and some jets, like the F-35B, can slow down and drop vertically. For most carrier jets, though, every landing still comes down to a hook, a wire and the pilot's nerve.

text: Heat always tries to move from hot things to cooler things. A flask slows that down. It has two walls, one inside the other, and the air between them has been pumped out to leave a [[vacuum|vacuum]]. Heat finds it very hard to cross empty space.
The inner walls are also shiny, so they bounce heat back towards the tea. A tight stopper stops warm steam escaping from the top. Together these tricks can keep a drink hot for hours.

sec.t:
Heat leaves a cup of tea in three ways. In conduction, heat passes from one particle to the next by touch, the way a steel spoon in tea gets hot at the handle. In convection, warm air or water rises and carries heat away, like steam curling off a cup. And in [[radiation|radiation]], heat travels as invisible [[infrared|infrared]] rays, the warmth you feel on your face from a fire across the room.

A good flask blocks all three. Most flasks also have a narrow neck, which leaves less room for heat to sneak out at the top. That is also why the stopper matters so much. Leave the lid off, and steam carries heat out of the opening far faster than it can leak through the walls. Every time you pour a cup, a little of that warmth escapes too.

sec.h: A scientist with a cold problem
sec.t:
James Dewar was a Scottish scientist working at the Royal Institution in London. In the 1890s he was turning gases like oxygen into liquids, which meant cooling them to about minus 200 °C. Ordinary containers let them boil away in minutes.

In 1892 he made a double-walled glass vessel with a vacuum between the walls, silvered to reflect heat. It kept his liquids cold for much longer. Dewar never patented it. In 1904 two German glassblowers started a company in Berlin to sell flasks to the public. They held a contest to name it, and the winner was Thermos.

Early flasks were made of thin [[@glass-made|glass]], which was easy to seal but broke if you dropped it. Many people in India remember carrying a flask with a fragile glass bottle inside a metal case on train journeys. Most flasks today are stainless steel, which is tougher, though slightly worse at holding heat.

Scientists still use large Dewar flasks to store liquid nitrogen. The same idea keeps [[vaccine|vaccines]] cold on long journeys to villages and helps hospitals carry blood and organs.

sec.h: Hot and cold, the same flask
sec.t:
A flask has no idea what is inside it. The vacuum slows heat flowing in as well as out. So on a summer day in Chennai or Phoenix, a flask of iced water stays chilled for hours.

A [[@refrigerator|refrigerator]] works in the opposite way, actively pumping heat out using electricity. A flask does nothing at all. It just makes heat take the slow road, and it never needs plugging in. Your body uses a similar trick when it keeps its [[@body-temperature|temperature]] steady, with fat and hair helping to hold warmth in.

text: Cheriyal scrolls are long, painted cloth scrolls from Cheriyal, a town in Telangana about 90 kilometres from [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]]. Each scroll is about a metre wide and can stretch 12 to 14 metres, about as long as a big school bus. It is split into about 50 scenes, one above the other, divided by flowery borders.

The scrolls were never meant to sit quietly in a museum. Travelling storytellers hung them up in village squares and sang the story while a helper pointed to each scene. The bright red backgrounds and big-eyed figures made the pictures easy to see by lamplight. Today the art survives mainly through a few families of painters in Cheriyal.

sec.h: Picture by picture, like a comic
sec.t:
Looked at from top to bottom, a scroll works much like a [[@comics-art|comic]]. Each panel shows one moment: a hero sets out, a demon attacks, a wedding takes place. Faces are drawn in profile with large eyes. Men, women, gods and animals are painted flat and bold, with no shadows.

The background is almost always red, with blues, yellows and greens on top. People living in the villages knew the stories already, so the pictures acted as a reminder. They followed the scenes, laughing and cheering at their favourite parts.

sec.h: Painting a scroll the old way
The singers who carried the scrolls
sec.t:
The paintings belong to the storytellers as much as to the painters. A community of balladeers called the Kaki Padagollu travelled with them. A team of about five would arrive in a village, tie the scroll to a frame of poles and perform with a harmonium, a drum and small clappers.

Different communities had their own stories, often about their own ancestors. Toddy tappers, leather workers and weavers each had a favourite tale. Mixed in were scenes from the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], the Mahabharata and tales of Krishna. A full performance could last several nights.

India has other painted scrolls with storytellers too. In Rajasthan, priests sing the tale of the folk hero Pabuji in front of a [[@art-phad|Phad]] painting. In Bengal, patuas sing as they unroll their scrolls. Each tradition looks different, but the idea is the same: a long picture and a singing voice.

As television and cinema spread, fewer villages invited the storytellers, and long scrolls became rare. To survive, Cheriyal painters began making smaller panels, single scenes and even key chains and masks for tourists. Their light masks, moulded from sawdust and tamarind seed paste, sell well too.

In 2008, Cheriyal paintings got a GI tag, a legal label that protects the name for art made in the region. And the strangest part? The way a scroll is read, one box after another, is the same trick used by every modern [[@graphic-novels|graphic novel]], centuries later.

text: The Indus (or Harappan) [[civilisation|civilisation]] flourished about 4,500 years ago, across today's [[@pakistan-history|India and Pakistan]]. Its cities were planned, with straight streets laid out in a grid, a bit like modern [[@chandigarh|Chandigarh]] or parts of New York.

Many houses had their own bathing area and toilet, connected to brick-lined drains that ran along the streets under stone or brick covers. Workers could lift the covers to clean out blockages. That is a system many cities in the world did not match for thousands of years.
Nobody knows for sure what they called themselves. Their writing hasn't been decoded.

spots: Brick-lined drains ran along streets and carried waste water away from homes.
Bricks in many cities followed the same shape: 1 part tall, 2 parts wide, 4 parts long. Very organised!

myth: Every great ancient civilisation was ruled by kings who built palaces and giant tombs.

Archaeologists have found no clear palaces, royal tombs or huge statues of rulers in Indus cities. Nobody knows exactly who was in charge, and some think power may have been shared among groups of leaders or merchants.

sec.t:
For thousands of years, the cities lay buried under mounds of earth. In the 1800s, railway builders even took old bricks from Harappa to lay under their tracks.

In 1921, the [[archaeologist|archaeologist]] Daya Ram Sahni began digging at Harappa, in today's Punjab province of Pakistan. In 1922, R.D. Banerji started at Mohenjo-daro, in Sindh. Soon the world realised that a forgotten civilisation, as old as Egypt and [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], had been found.

Builders used baked bricks of the same 1:2:4 shape everywhere. Merchants used stone weights in a standard set of sizes, doubling from small to large, so a sack of grain weighed the same in Harappa as in Lothal.

Wells were dug all over the cities. Mohenjo-daro may have had hundreds. Houses faced side lanes instead of the main streets, perhaps for privacy and to keep out dust. Many [[@toilets-sewers|modern sewers]] still use the same basic idea of sloping, covered channels.

Indus people made beads, pottery, [[@clothes-cotton|cotton]] cloth and stone seals. Their carnelian beads, drilled with long, fine holes, have been found far away in [[@harappan-trade|Mesopotamia]], in today's Iraq. Mesopotamian writings mention a land called Meluhha, which many scholars think was the Indus region.

Artists also cast small bronze figures. The most famous, known as the "Dancing Girl", is in the National Museum in New Delhi. A stone bust of a bearded man, nicknamed the "Priest-King", was found at Mohenjo-daro and is now in Pakistan.

Farmers grew wheat, barley, peas and sesame, and some of the world's earliest cotton. They kept cattle, [[@goats-sheep|sheep and goats]].

After about 1900 BCE, the big cities slowly emptied, as people moved to smaller villages. Experts still debate why. Rivers may have changed course or dried up, and the [[monsoon|monsoon]] may have weakened, making farming harder. It was probably a mix of causes over many years, not a sudden disaster.

We can't yet read their [[@writing-began|writing]], so much of their story is told by the cities themselves. Their seals show animals like bulls, elephants and a one-horned creature, next to short rows of signs. Whoever cracks the code will open a door that has been shut for 4,000 years.

text: When the last fluent speaker of a language dies, the language stops being used for everyday talk. Linguists call it [[extinct|extinct]] or dormant. If nobody recorded it, the words, grammar, songs and stories may be lost for ever. If people did make recordings and dictionaries, it might one day be woken up again.

There are about 7,000 languages in the world, but most are spoken by small groups. The language guide Ethnologue estimates that roughly 40 percent are [[endangered|endangered]], usually because children are growing up speaking a bigger language instead. Linguists disagree about how fast languages are disappearing, but they agree it is happening across every continent.

myth: When a language disappears, nothing important is lost, because people can say the same things in another language.

Every language carries knowledge that may not translate easily, such as names for plants and medicines, ways of counting, songs, stories and jokes. When it vanishes without records, much of that knowledge can vanish too.

sec.t:
Languages rarely vanish because people suddenly stop speaking. They fade over generations. Parents may feel their children will get better jobs if they speak a major language, such as English, Hindi or Spanish. Schools may teach only in the big language. Sometimes, as with many [[@myths-native-american|Native American languages]] in the USA, children were punished at boarding schools for speaking their own.

India is home to hundreds of languages. UNESCO's atlas lists nearly 200 Indian languages as endangered, more than any other country. Many belong to small [[@people-tribes-india|tribal communities]] whose children now study in a regional language and English.

Every language carries a particular way of seeing the world. Some languages have no words for left and right, using north, south, east and west instead, even for things on a table. Others have dozens of words for kinds of rain, fish or forest plants, and some of those names record which plants heal and which ones poison.

When a language dies, that knowledge does not always move into the new language. A word can carry a whole story inside it, and a story can hold the memory of a flood, a migration or a star that guided sailors.

Sometimes a language comes back. The most famous case is Hebrew. In the late 1800s, people in what is now Israel began speaking it at home again, and today millions use it every day.

In the USA, a Wampanoag woman named Jessie Little Doe Baird studied old documents, including a Bible translated into her people's language in the 1600s. She helped bring Wampanoag back, and her daughter became one of its first native speakers in about a century. In the Isle of Man, Manx lost its last native speaker in 1974, but a Manx-language primary school now teaches children in it.

Linguists record elders, write grammars and build dictionaries, sometimes in a race against time. Apps, keyboards and online videos help young people use small languages on their phones. Some researchers are working on [[@translation-apps|translation apps]] for languages with only a few thousand speakers.

None of that works without speakers who care. The strongest protection for a language is children who use it with their friends. Even languages that need no voice at all can be in danger, as you can see with [[@sign-language|sign languages]] around the world.

text: The Earth takes about 365 days, 5 hours and 49 minutes to go once round the Sun. Calendars can only count whole days, so a normal year has 365. That leaves almost a quarter of a day over each year.

If we ignored it, the calendar would slip by about one day every four years. After a century, it would be nearly a month out. Summer holidays would slowly drift into the rains, and festivals tied to the seasons would land at the wrong time.
So every four years we add an extra day, [[@calendar-maths|29 February]]. That year has 366 days and is called a leap year.

st.prompt: Will the year 2100 be a leap year?

Nobody has decided yet

st.reveal: Century years are leap years only if they divide exactly by 400. So 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 wasn't and 2100 won't be. Skipping these three leap days every 400 years keeps the calendar in step with the seasons.

Historians have found little real evidence of such riots. The slogan appears on a banner in a famous painting by William Hogarth about an election, and the riot story seems to have grown from that.

sec.t:
Julius Caesar's calendar, started in 45 BCE, used this simple rule: one leap year every four years, no exceptions. That makes the average year exactly 365¼ days.

But the real year is about 11 minutes shorter than that. Eleven minutes doesn't sound like much. Over 128 years it adds up to a whole day. By the 1500s, the calendar had drifted about ten days away from the [[@seasons-why|seasons]]. Easter, which depends on the spring [[equinox|equinox]], was moving out of place.

In 1582, Pope Gregory XIII introduced a corrected calendar, worked out by a team of [[astronomer|astronomers]]. It did two things.

First, it jumped forward ten days to catch up. In Italy, [[@spain|Spain]] and a few other countries, Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October.

Second, it made a small change to the leap year rule. Century years would only be leap years if they divided exactly by 400. That removes three leap days every 400 years. The average year becomes 365.2425 days, very close to the real one. The Gregorian calendar only drifts by about one day in 3,000 years.

{{story:seasons-why}}

Not every country switched at once. Protestant Britain was suspicious of a calendar made by a pope and waited 170 years. By then the gap had grown to [[@oddity-calendar-missing-days|11 days]].

In 1752, Britain and all its colonies, including the American colonies and the [[territory|territories]] ruled by the British [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] in India, made the jump. Wednesday 2 September 1752 was followed directly by Thursday 14 September.

Some countries switched even later. [[@russia|Russia]] changed only in 1918, after its revolution. The Russian Orthodox Church still uses the older Julian calendar for its festivals, so its [[@christmas|Christmas]] falls on 7 January.

A baby born on 29 February only gets a real birthday every four years. Such people are sometimes called "leaplings". The chance of being born on that day is about 1 in 1,461, because there are 1,461 days in every four-year cycle.

In common years, most leaplings celebrate on 28 February or 1 March. Some joke that they are only a quarter of their real age.

Leap days keep the calendar in step with the Sun. A different problem is the length of a single day. The Earth's spin is not perfectly steady, and over long periods it is slowly getting longer.

Since 1972, timekeepers have occasionally added a "leap second" to the world's clocks to keep them matched with the Earth's spin. These extra seconds cause headaches for computers, so scientists have agreed to stop adding them by 2035. Other calendars solve the same kind of problem in their own way. Many [[@indian-calendars|Indian calendars]] add a whole extra month every few years instead of a single day.

text: The Grand Slams are the four biggest [[tournament|tournaments]] in tennis: the Australian Open, the French Open, Wimbledon and the US Open. They are the oldest, offer the most prize money and ranking points, and are the titles players want most.

Each one is played on a different kind of court, in a different city, at a different time of year. A player who wins all four in the same calendar year has "won the Grand Slam", one of the hardest feats in sport. Winning all four over a whole career is called a career Grand Slam.

Each of the four is called a Grand Slam tournament. But strictly, "winning the Grand Slam" means winning all four in the same calendar year. Winning all four at different times in a career is called a career Grand Slam.

sec.t:
The season starts in January with the **Australian Open** in Melbourne, played on hard courts in the middle of the Australian summer. Temperatures sometimes pass 40 °C, so there are rules for stopping play in extreme heat.

In late May comes the **French Open**, or Roland-Garros, in [[@paris|Paris]]. It is played on clay made of crushed brick, which slows the ball and makes it bounce high. Long rallies and sliding players are part of its style. Next is **Wimbledon** in [[@london|London]], in late June and July, on grass, where the ball skids and stays low. Players must wear almost all white. The year ends with the **US Open** in New York in late August, on hard courts, often under floodlights late at night.

Only two men have won all four singles titles in a calendar year. Don Budge of the USA did it in 1938, and Rod Laver of Australia did it twice, in 1962 and 1969. Three women have done it: Maureen Connolly in 1953, Margaret Court in 1970, and Steffi Graf in 1988. Graf also won Olympic gold that year, a feat called the Golden Slam.

Until 1968, the Grand Slams were only for amateurs, and the best professionals were shut out. Since then, in what is called the Open Era, records have kept climbing. Novak Djokovic has won 24 men's singles titles, the most ever (as of 2026). Margaret Court won 24 women's singles titles, though many came before 1968. [[@serena-williams|Serena Williams]] won 23, the most of the Open Era.

India's best Grand Slam results have come in doubles. In 1997, Mahesh Bhupathi and Rika Hiraki of Japan won the French Open mixed doubles, making Bhupathi the first Indian Grand Slam champion. He and Leander Paes went on to win many doubles titles, together and with other partners.

Sania Mirza won six Grand Slam doubles titles, three in women's doubles and three in mixed. In 2024, Rohan Bopanna won the Australian Open men's doubles at the age of 43, the oldest man to win a Grand Slam title in the Open Era. In singles, Ramanathan Krishnan reached the Wimbledon semi-finals in 1960 and 1961.

The Slams have changed a lot. The US Open became the first Slam to use electronic line-calling replays, called Hawk-Eye, in 2006. In 2025, Wimbledon replaced its line judges with electronic line-calling for the first time in its history. Some fans missed the human voices shouting "Out!" The grass, the white clothes and the strawberries and cream, though, are still there.

text: A roller coaster is a lesson in energy. A chain or cable drags the train slowly up the first hill. At the top, the train has stored energy simply because it is high up. When it tips over the edge, [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] pulls it down, and that stored energy turns into speed.

At the bottom, the speed carries the train up the next hill, where it slows and stores energy again. Back and forth, the energy swaps between height and speed until the ride ends. A little is lost all the time to [[@friction|friction]] and air resistance, which is why the brakes at the end only have to stop a train that is already slowing.

st.prompt: Why is the first hill of a classic roller coaster usually the tallest?

options.t: The train has no engine, so every later hill must be lower
To give riders the best view of the park
Because the builders run out of steel later

st.reveal: The chain lift gives the train all the energy it will have. As it rolls, friction and air resistance slowly use some up. So each hill after the first must be a bit lower, or the train would stall.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, roller coaster.
Halliday D., Resnick R. and Walker J., Fundamentals of Physics (chapters on energy and circular motion).

myth: Roller coaster loops are perfect circles.

Most modern loops are teardrop-shaped, tighter at the top and wider at the bottom. A circular loop would need the train to enter it much faster, which would push riders hard into their seats at the bottom.

sec.t:
Coasters began with sleds. In [[@russia|Russia]], by the 1600s, people built wooden ramps covered in ice and slid down them in winter. Later, wheeled carts on tracks let the fun continue in summer.

In 1884, LaMarcus Adna Thompson opened the Switchback Railway at Coney Island in [[@new-york|New York]]. Riders paid a few cents to roll down a gentle wooden track at about the speed of a bicycle. Within a few decades, America had hundreds of wooden coasters, and the race to build higher and faster rides was on.

India's first big amusement parks came later. EsselWorld in Mumbai opened in 1989, and parks such as Wonderla in Bengaluru followed.

{{story:gravity-fall}}

Over the top of a hill, the track curves away beneath you. Your body wants to keep going in a straight line, so for a moment you float slightly off the seat. Riders call this "airtime". At the bottom of a dip, the opposite happens and you feel pressed down, heavier than usual.

Engineers measure these pushes in "g". One g is what you feel sitting still. Many coasters reach about 4 g at the bottom of a drop, so for a second you feel four times heavier. Your inner ear, which helps with balance, notices every change. That is part of why your stomach seems to flip.

sec.h: Keeping the train on the track
sec.t:
Each car has three sets of wheels. Running wheels sit on top of the rail and carry the weight. Side wheels stop it sliding left or right. Upstop wheels sit under the rail, so the car cannot lift off over a hill or hang loose upside down.

Loops use a teardrop shape so that the curve is tight at the top, where the train is slow, and gentle at the bottom, where it is fast. This keeps the forces on riders within safe limits. The first modern coaster with a [[@how-roller-coaster-loop|teardrop loop]], Revolution, opened in California in 1976. Before that, a few loop coasters in the early 1900s used round loops, and riders complained of sore necks.

Some coasters skip the chain lift and fire the train forward instead. Some use powerful hydraulic motors. Others use linear motors, rows of electromagnets along the track that push and pull on metal fins under the car, a little like [[@magnets-how|magnets]] chasing each other in a line.

Formula Rossa at Ferrari World in Abu Dhabi uses a hydraulic launch. It reaches about 240 km/h in under five seconds, faster than most cars on a motorway. For years it was the fastest coaster in the world, until Falcons Flight in Saudi Arabia opened at the end of 2025 with a top speed of about 250 km/h. Riders wear goggles, because at that speed even a small insect hitting your eye would hurt.

text: You see because light bounces off things and into your eyes. It passes through the clear front window of the eye, the [[cornea|cornea]], and through the black hole in the middle, the pupil. Behind the pupil sits a soft, clear lens that focuses the light into a sharp picture.

That picture lands on the [[retina|retina]], a thin layer at the back of the eye packed with light-sensing cells. They turn light into electrical signals, which travel along the optic nerve to the back of your brain.
Your brain does the rest. It flips the image the right way up, joins the views from both eyes, and works out what you're looking at.

options.t: Upside down
The right way up

st.reveal: Upside down. A curved lens bends light so that rays from the top of a scene land at the bottom of the retina, and the other way round. Your brain has learned to make sense of this, so the world looks the right way up.

myth: Eating lots of carrots gives you super night vision.

Carrots contain a substance the body turns into vitamin A, which the eyes need to see in dim light. People who lack vitamin A can develop night blindness, so carrots help them. But if you already get enough, extra carrots won't let you see in the dark.

sec.t:
An eye works a lot like a [[@cameras-how|camera]]. The cornea and lens focus light, as a camera's lens does. The iris, [[@body-eye-colour-babies|the coloured ring]], is a [[@muscles|muscle]] that widens or narrows the pupil, letting in more light in a dim room and less in bright sunshine. The retina is like the camera's [[sensor|sensor]].

The eyeball is filled with a clear jelly that keeps its round shape. An adult eye is about 2.4 cm across, about the size of a large grape.

To focus on something close, like this screen, tiny muscles change the lens's shape. As people reach their forties, the lens stiffens, which is why many grandparents hold a newspaper at arm's length or wear reading [[@lenses-glasses|glasses]].

Where the optic nerve leaves the eye, there's no room for rods or cones. That patch is blind. You don't notice because your other eye covers it, and your brain paints in the gap using the colours and patterns around it. Try the card trick below to find yours.

Some ancient Greek thinkers believed the eyes sent out rays to touch what they saw. Around 1,000 years ago, the scientist Ibn al-Haytham, working in Cairo, argued from experiments that light travels into the eye instead. His *Book of Optics* shaped science in the Islamic world and Europe for centuries.

In ancient India, the surgical text linked to [[@sushruta|Sushruta]] describes an operation for cataract, when the lens becomes cloudy. Today cataract surgery replaces the cloudy lens with a plastic one, and it's one of the most common operations in both India and the USA.

Many children are short-sighted: they see near things clearly but faraway things look blurry, like the board at school. The eyeball has grown a little too long, so light focuses in front of the retina. Glasses fix this by bending the light before it enters. Studies suggest that spending more time playing outdoors in daylight lowers children's chances of becoming short-sighted.

[[@owl-silent|Owls]] have huge eyes packed with rods for hunting at night, but they can't move them in their sockets, so they swivel their heads instead. [[@eagles-hunt|Eagles]] see fine detail much farther away than we can. Every one of these eyes uses the same basic trick: a lens, a screen of sensors and a brain to make sense of it.

text: For most people, a short nap is good for you. A rest of about 10 to 20 minutes in the early afternoon can make you more alert, improve your mood and help your brain hold on to things you learned that morning.

Longer naps are trickier. Sleep for an hour or more and you may wake up groggy, and a late or long nap can make it harder to fall asleep at night. For children, the most important sleep is still a full night's rest. Naps are a bonus, not a replacement.

st.reveal: After about 20 to 30 minutes, the brain often slides into deep sleep. Waking up in the middle of it causes "sleep inertia", a heavy, confused feeling that can last a while. Short naps usually end before deep sleep begins.

src.Rosekind M. R. et al. (1994) Crew Factor: Effects of Planned Cockpit Rest on Crew Performance and Alertness in Long-Haul Operations, NASA Technical Memorandum 108839.

Short naps can sharpen attention and memory at any age. Pilots, doctors on long shifts, athletes and astronauts use planned naps to stay alert and safe.

sec.t:
Many people feel sleepy in the early afternoon, often after lunch. Food plays a small part, but the main reason is your [[@body-clock|body clock]]. Your alertness naturally rises and falls through the day, and for most people there is a small dip between about 1 and 3 p.m.

In many warm countries, people have long built a rest into the day. Spain is famous for the siesta. In parts of India, shops in small towns may close for a couple of hours after lunch while people rest through the hottest part of the day. In [[@japan-culture|Japan]], a short doze at a desk, on a train or even in a meeting is called *inemuri*. It has often been seen as a sign that someone is working very hard, not that they are lazy.

Sleep comes in stages. In the first few minutes, you drift into light sleep. After about 20 to 30 minutes, you may slip into deep sleep, when the brain slows right down. If you wake up from deep sleep, you can feel heavy and confused for a while. Scientists call this sleep [[inertia|inertia]].

A nap of 10 to 20 minutes usually ends before deep sleep begins, so you wake up feeling fresher. A much longer nap of about 90 minutes can take you through a full sleep cycle, including [[@dreams|dreaming]], but it is more likely to disturb your sleep that night.

Researchers have found that a nap after learning something new, such as a list of words or a new skill, can help people remember it better later. During sleep, the brain seems to sort and store the day's experiences, moving them into longer-term [[@memory|memory]].

This doesn't mean you can skip studying and just sleep. But a short rest between learning sessions may help.

Babies sleep for much of the day. Toddlers usually nap once or twice a day, and most children stop napping regularly somewhere between about 3 and 5 years old. Children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night, and teenagers about 8 to 10.

If a school-age child feels very sleepy every afternoon, the cause is often too little sleep at night, perhaps from late screen time or early school starts. Going to bed at a regular time usually helps more than daytime napping. If tiredness goes on for a long time, it is worth talking to a parent or a doctor.

text: Assistive technology is any tool that helps a disabled person do something that would otherwise be hard or impossible. Some tools are simple, like a ramp or a large-print book. Others are high-tech: [[@blindness-tech|phones that read the screen aloud]], [[@computer-vision|glasses that describe what they see]], and computers controlled with the eyes.

A good example is the screen reader. It turns everything on a screen into speech or [[@braille|braille]]. On a touchscreen, a blind person slides a finger around and the phone says what's underneath. A double tap selects it. With practice, many users set the voice to talk so fast that it sounds like a blur to everyone else.

st.prompt: How does a blind person use a touchscreen phone with no buttons to feel?

st.reveal: Phones have built-in screen readers, such as VoiceOver and TalkBack. Moving a finger across the screen reads out each item, and a double tap opens it. Many users speed the voice up so fast that others can't follow it.

myth: Accessibility features only help a small number of people.

About one in six people worldwide has a significant disability, and almost everyone will need some help as they age. Features designed for disabled people, such as ramps, captions and voice control, end up helping parents with prams, travellers, and anyone in a noisy room.

sec.t:
For deaf and hard-of-hearing people, captions turn speech into text on a screen. Phones can now caption almost any video or call live, using speech recognition. Video calling has made [[@sign-language|sign language]] much easier to use at a distance, since two signers can now see each other's hands from anywhere.

Flashing doorbells, vibrating alarm clocks and phones that buzz in patterns help people who can't hear sounds. [[@hearing-aids|Hearing aids]] and cochlear implants help others hear better.

People who can't move their hands can control computers in other ways. Eye-tracking cameras watch where someone looks and move a pointer there. Switches can be pressed with the head, a foot or a puff of breath, stepping through options one by one. [[@voice-assistants|Voice assistants]] let people turn on lights, make calls and write messages by speaking.

Some people with conditions that affect speech use communication devices that speak for them. Researchers are even testing [[@future-brain-computer|brain implants]] that let paralysed people move a cursor just by thinking.

Technology only helps if buildings, websites and services are designed for everyone. The Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 requires public places and many businesses in the United States to be accessible. India's Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act of 2016 does something similar, and the Accessible India Campaign, launched in 2015, works on making government buildings, transport and websites easier to use.

Websites can be built so that screen readers understand them, with labels on buttons and descriptions of pictures. Many still aren't, which shuts people out of shopping, banking and schoolwork. Making cities and schools work for everyone is the idea behind [[@disabilities-inclusion|inclusion]].

In the United States, campaigners in the 1970s pushed cities to cut slopes into the kerbs at street corners, so wheelchair users could cross. Soon parents with prams, travellers with suitcases and delivery workers with trolleys were using them too. People now call this the curb-cut effect.

The same thing happens with technology. Captions help people learning a language and anyone watching on a noisy train. Voice typing helps busy cooks. Audiobooks, first recorded for blind readers in the 1930s, are now enjoyed by millions of commuters. Designing for disability often means designing better for all.

text: Inside a smartwatch is a tiny [[sensor|sensor]] called an accelerometer. It measures how fast the watch speeds up or slows down, in three directions at once: up and down, side to side, and forwards and back. Every time your foot hits the ground, your whole body jolts, and your wrist jolts with it.

When you walk, those jolts come in a steady [[rhythm|rhythm]], about one or two every second. The watch runs a small set of rules, an [[@algorithms|algorithm]], that looks for that rhythm. If a jolt is strong enough and arrives at about the right moment after the last one, the watch counts a step. Random shakes, like waving at a friend, mostly get ignored.

st.prompt: You sit in a bumpy autorickshaw ride for twenty minutes with your watch on. What might happen to your step count?

options.t: It might go up, even though you didn't walk
It stays exactly the same, because the watch knows you are sitting
It goes down, because the watch subtracts the bumps

st.reveal: Bumps can look a lot like the rhythmic jolts of walking. Good watches filter out most of them, but some sneak through as extra steps. Pushing a pram or a shopping trolley can do the opposite, because your arm stays still.

myth: Scientists worked out that 10,000 steps a day is the right amount for health.

The number came from the name of a Japanese pedometer called manpo-kei, which means "10,000-step meter". Large studies since then suggest the benefits start to level off somewhere between about 6,000 and 10,000 steps a day, depending on age.

sec.h: A weight on a spring, shrunk to a chip
sec.t:
The accelerometer works like a tiny weight held by [[@springs|springs]]. When the watch moves, the weight lags behind for a moment, the way your body tips back when a bus pulls away. The chip measures how far the weight shifts and turns that into a number.

All of this is carved into silicon only a few millimetres across, using the same methods that make [[@chips-silicon|computer chips]]. Many watches add a gyroscope, which senses twisting, so the watch can tell a step from a turn of the wrist. Some also carry [[@gps-how|GPS]] to measure how far you went outdoors.

Turn many smartwatches over and you'll see small green lights flashing. Blood absorbs green light well. Each time [[@heart-health|your heart beats]], a little more blood pushes into the tiny vessels in your wrist, and a little less light bounces back to a sensor beside the LEDs.

By timing those dips, the watch estimates your heart rate. It's a neat trick, but it struggles when the strap is loose, when you're moving very fast, or in cold weather when less blood flows to the skin. That's why the numbers can jump around during a sprint.

In 1965, a Japanese company sold a pedometer called manpo-kei, which means "10,000-step meter". The round number was catchy, and it stuck for decades.

Researchers have since tested it. A large review of studies, published in 2022, found that people who walk more do tend to live longer. But the extra benefit starts to flatten out somewhere between about 6,000 and 10,000 steps a day. Older adults reached that point sooner than younger ones. For a [[@exercise|healthy body]], the exact number matters less than moving often.

Fitbit's first tracker, which clipped onto [[@future-clothes|clothing]], went on sale in 2009. Today the same idea sits on millions of wrists, and inside most [[@smartphones|smartphones]] too, quietly counting while you get on with your day.

text: It was the morning of 2 July 1937. Amelia Earhart radioed one of her last messages: "We must be on you, but cannot see you." Then silence. She and her navigator, Fred Noonan, were hunting for Howland Island, a tiny dot in the Pacific. They never arrived.

Nobody knows exactly what happened. The most widely accepted idea is that their plane ran out of fuel and sank into water more than 5 km deep. A second idea says they landed on a reef at another island, Nikumaroro, and lived there for a while as castaways. Almost ninety years of searching have not settled it.

st.prompt: Earhart was trying to find Howland Island in the middle of the Pacific. How big is it?

options.t: About 2.5 km long, smaller than many airports
About as big as Sri Lanka
About as big as Mumbai

st.reveal: Howland Island is a flat speck about 2.5 km long and less than 1 km wide. From the air, in hazy morning light, it could easily hide among cloud shadows on the sea.

n.certNote: Nobody knows for sure. Most aviation experts think the plane ran out of fuel and sank near Howland Island. Some researchers argue that Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumaroro and died there as castaways.

myth: Amelia Earhart was captured by Japanese soldiers, and a photo proves it.
A photo said to show her on a Pacific dock in 1937 was later found printed in a Japanese travel book from 1935, two years before she disappeared. There is no good evidence that she was captured.
facts: Amelia Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan
Howland Island, a strip of land about 2.5 km long

sec.t:
By 1937, Earhart was a superstar. In 1932 she became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, in about 15 hours. She wrote books, gave talks and designed her own range of clothes.

Then she set out to fly around the world along its fattest part, close to the [[equator|equator]]. That meant about 47,000 km. Her silver [[@airplanes-fly|Lockheed Electra]] left Miami on 1 June 1937 and flew east across South America, Africa and Asia.

On the way she landed in Karachi, then in Calcutta (now Kolkata), where [[monsoon|monsoon]] rain soaked the airfield. Less than two weeks later she reached Lae, in New Guinea. Only about 11,000 km remained, but the hardest leg came first.

sec.h: A speck in a very big ocean
sec.t:
From Lae to Howland is about 4,100 km of open water. There were no satellites and no [[@gps-how|GPS]]. Noonan used the stars, a compass, a clock and maths to guess their position.

Howland was so small that a navy ship, the *Itasca*, waited beside it to guide her by [[@radio-waves|radio]]. The ship could hear Earhart, but she seemed unable to hear it. Her radio direction finder never locked on. Her calls grew louder, which meant she was close, and then they stopped.

Some radio listeners far away, from Florida to Canada, later said they had picked up faint calls from a woman in the days after. Nobody could prove the calls were real.

The US Navy and Coast Guard searched about 650,000 square kilometres of ocean. That is an area about the size of Texas. They found nothing.

{{story:wright-brothers}}

sec.h: Theory one: down in the deep
sec.t:
Most experts think the Electra ran low on fuel, dropped into the sea near Howland and sank. The water there is deep and dark. Finding a small plane on that seabed is like finding a car on the floor of a sea as wide as a country.

In 2024, a company called Deep Sea Vision released a sonar picture that looked like a plane. A closer look later that year showed it was a rock.

sec.h: Theory two: castaways on a reef
sec.t:
Nikumaroro is a coral [[atoll|atoll]] about 650 km southeast of Howland. In 1940, a British officer found part of a skeleton there, along with a woman's shoe sole and a box made for a sextant, a tool for navigating by the stars. The bones were measured by a doctor, then lost.

A group called TIGHAR has led more than a dozen trips to the island since 1989. In October 2026, a team from Purdue University checked a plane-shaped blur in the [[lagoon|lagoon]]. It turned out to be a pile of old tree trunks.

Earhart's plane is one of the most hunted objects on Earth. Every new satellite photo, sonar scan or rusty piece of metal brings a fresh wave of hope. Strange disappearances at sea have always gripped people. The oddest of all may be the ship found drifting in 1872 with its crew gone and their belongings still aboard: the [[@mystery-mary-celeste|Mary Celeste]].

text: About 2,500 years ago, a prince named [[@buddha|Siddhartha Gautama]] left his comfortable life to find out why people suffer. After years of searching, he sat down under a peepal tree near the Niranjana river and decided not to get up until he understood. Buddhists believe that there, on a full-moon night, he reached enlightenment, a deep understanding of life. From then on he was called the Buddha, "the awakened one".

That spot is now Bodh Gaya, in Bihar. For Buddhists it is the holiest place on Earth. Monks and visitors arrive from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Japan, Tibet, Myanmar, the USA and dozens of other countries to sit, chant and walk around the tree.

st.prompt: The Buddha is said to have meditated under a Bodhi tree. What kind of tree is it?

options.t: A peepal, also called a sacred fig
A banyan
A neem

st.reveal: The Bodhi tree is a peepal, a kind of fig with heart-shaped leaves that end in a long, thin tip. Peepal trees are also sacred in Hinduism, and you will often see them near temples and village squares.

n.certNote: Most historians accept that the Buddha lived about 2,500 years ago, but his exact dates are debated. The present Bodhi tree is believed, not proven, to descend from the original through a cutting kept in Sri Lanka.

myth: The Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya is the very same tree the Buddha sat under.
The original tree died long ago. The tree there today is believed to have grown from a cutting of the Sri Maha Bodhi in Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka, which itself grew from a branch of the first tree.
facts: Buddhists, and visited by many Hindus

sec.h: A tree with a family history
sec.t:
The Emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]], who became a Buddhist after a terrible war, visited Bodh Gaya in the 3rd century BCE. Buddhist tradition says his daughter Sanghamitta carried a branch of the Bodhi tree to [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], where it was planted at Anuradhapura. That tree still grows there and is one of the oldest planted trees with a recorded history.

Over the centuries, the tree in Bodh Gaya was damaged and replaced more than once. In the 1880s, a cutting was brought back from Sri Lanka and planted on the old spot. So the tree you see today is probably a grandchild of the first.

After Buddhism faded in much of India, Bodh Gaya was neglected for hundreds of years. The temple fell into ruin and was partly buried. In the 1880s, British [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] led by Alexander Cunningham, with help from the king of Burma, repaired it.

A Sri Lankan Buddhist named Anagarika Dharmapala visited in 1891 and was upset to find the temple in poor shape. He started the Maha Bodhi Society to campaign for Buddhists to look after it. Since 1949, a committee with both Buddhist and Hindu members has managed the temple. Some Buddhists still campaign for it to be run by Buddhists alone, while others are content with the shared arrangement.

Walk around Bodh Gaya today and it feels like a world tour. Thailand, Bhutan, Japan, Tibet, Vietnam and other countries have built [[monastery|monasteries]] here, each in its own style. One looks like a Thai palace with a gold roof, while another has a Japanese garden.

The ruins of [[@nalanda|Nalanda]], once a great centre of Buddhist learning, are about 80 km away. Pilgrims often visit both, along with Rajgir nearby, where the Buddha spent many rainy seasons teaching.

The biggest day of the year in Bodh Gaya is Buddha Purnima, the full moon of the month of Vaishakha, which usually falls in April or May. Many Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death together on that day. The town fills with monks in maroon, saffron and grey robes, chanting in Pali, Tibetan, Japanese and many other languages.

Winter is busy too, when the weather is cool and Tibetan Buddhists arrive in large numbers. Nearby stands the Great Buddha Statue, a seated figure about 25 metres tall that was unveiled in 1989. Children from local villages sell beads and lotus flowers to visitors, and the sound of bells carries across the town.

text: The White House is the home and office of the President of the United States. It stands at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in [[@washington-dc|Washington, D.C.]], the US capital. Every president since John Adams in 1800 has lived there.

It is also a working office, a museum and a symbol. When news reports say "the White House said today", they mean the president and their staff. Its picture appears on the back of the US $20 note, so most Americans carry it around without thinking about it.

st.prompt: In 1814 something happened to the White House that forced the president to move out for years. What was it?

options.t: British soldiers set it on fire during a war
An earthquake knocked down its walls
A flood from the Potomac River filled it with mud

st.reveal: During the War of 1812, British troops captured Washington and burned the White House and the Capitol. Only the scorched outer walls survived. It took about three years to rebuild.

myth: The White House was painted white to hide the burn marks after the fire of 1814.
Its stone walls were first coated with white lime wash in 1798, years before the fire, to protect them from rain and frost. People were already calling it the White House before 1814.

sec.t:
In 1792, a competition was held to design a home for the president. It was won by James Hoban, an architect born in Ireland. His plan was for a large, elegant house of pale sandstone, inspired by country houses in Ireland and Britain.

[[@george-washington|George Washington]] chose the site and approved the design, but the house was not ready until 1800, after his term ended. It was built by a mix of workers: hired labourers, skilled stonemasons from Scotland and enslaved African Americans, whose work is now recognised by historians and by the White House itself. The outside was coated with a lime-based whitewash to protect the stone.

The main residence has 132 rooms, 35 bathrooms and six levels, including two basement floors. It also has 28 fireplaces and 147 windows. The ground and first floors include famous rooms open to visitors, such as the Blue Room, the Red Room and the long East Room, used for big ceremonies. The president's family lives on the floors above.

The West Wing, added in 1902, holds offices for the president's staff. The Oval Office, the president's own office, was added to it in 1909. Its oval shape echoes oval rooms in the main house. Between 1949 and 1952, the inside of the main house was almost completely rebuilt, because its old wooden beams were close to collapse. President Harry Truman and his family moved across the street while workers kept only the outer walls and built a steel frame inside them.

Every president changes something. Some have added tennis courts, a swimming pool or a vegetable garden. In October 2025, the East Wing was demolished to make room for a large new ballroom, a project that drew both support and criticism.

Some traditions last. Since 1878, children have raced to push eggs across the South Lawn with spoons at the Easter Egg Roll. Presidents have hosted Diwali celebrations at the White House since 2003, and the lighting of diyas there is now a regular event for many [[@indian-diaspora|Indian Americans]].

sec.h: A house for the whole country
sec.t: In India, the President lives in the Rashtrapati Bhavan in New Delhi, which is far larger than the White House. The White House was meant to be grand but not a palace, a house fit for a citizen rather than a king. That idea, a leader who lives among the people and leaves after their term, is part of what the building stands for.

text: Mark Twain was the pen name of Samuel Clemens, an American writer and humorist who lived from 1835 to 1910. He wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, two of the most famous American novels.

Twain wrote the way people really talked, with their slang and accents. Before him, a lot of American writers tried to sound like the English. He was also one of the funniest writers of his time. He gave lectures all over the world, and people paid to hear him tell stories.

Danger, rocks ahead
Two boats are passing each other

st.reveal: Crew members measured depth with a weighted rope. "Twain" is an old word for two, and a fathom is about 1.8 metres. Two fathoms, about 3.7 metres, was deep enough for a steamboat, so the call meant safe water.

myth: Mark Twain said, "The reports of my death are greatly exaggerated."
In 1897 a newspaper wrongly reported that he was dying. He wrote that "the report of my death was an exaggeration". The punchier version became popular later.
facts: Hannibal, Missouri, on the Mississippi River
The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn

sec.t:
Clemens grew up in Hannibal, a small town in Missouri on the banks of the Mississippi, one of the [[@rivers-longest|longest rivers]] in North America. Steamboats churned past, and every boy in town, he later wrote, wanted to work on one.

His father died when he was eleven, and he left school to work for a printer. In his twenties he trained as a steamboat pilot, memorising every sandbar and bend over more than 1,000 km of river. He got his licence in 1859. The river shaped his best books and gave him his name.

The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) is about a mischievous boy in a river town much like Hannibal. In one famous scene, Tom is told to whitewash a fence. He pretends it is such fun that other boys pay him for a turn.

Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884) is darker. Huck, Tom's friend, runs away from his violent father and floats down the river on a raft with Jim, a man escaping slavery. As they travel, Huck slowly realises that everything his society taught him about Jim is wrong. The novelist Ernest Hemingway later said that all modern American writing comes from this one book.

The book has also caused arguments. It uses a racist word many times, because that is how people in the story spoke before the Civil War. Some schools in the US have removed it from reading lists. Others teach it as a powerful attack on racism and [[@slavery-freedom|slavery]]. Readers still disagree about how it should be taught.

{{story:comets}}

In 1895 and 1896, deep in debt, Twain went on a lecture tour around the world. He spent about two months in India in 1896, visiting Bombay, Calcutta, [[@varanasi|Varanasi]], Agra and Darjeeling. He wrote about it in his travel book Following the Equator (1897).

He was dazzled by India's crowds, colours and history, and wrote that it was the most extraordinary country under the sun. He also wrote about the [[@taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]], the ghats of Varanasi and a ride down the mountain from Darjeeling on a little open railway car. He called that the most enjoyable day he had ever spent.

sec.h: Born and gone with a comet
sec.t:
Twain was born in November 1835, just after Halley's Comet passed close to Earth. The [[@comets|comet]] returns about every 76 years. In 1909 he joked that he had come in with it and expected to go out with it. He died on 21 April 1910, one day after the comet's closest approach to the Sun.

Twain lived much of his later life in Hartford, Connecticut, where his house is now a museum. His quick sayings are quoted so often that many lines he never said get stuck to his name too.

text: Most sugar comes from two plants: sugarcane, a giant grass that grows in warm places, and sugar beet, a pale root grown in cool countries. Like all green plants, they make sugar from sunlight, water and air through [[@photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. They simply store much more of it than most plants.

At a sugar mill, cane is crushed to squeeze out its juice. The juice is cleaned, boiled down until it is thick and syrupy, and spun in machines so that sugar [[crystal|crystals]] separate from the dark syrup, called [[@oddity-great-molasses-flood|molasses]]. Further cleaning turns brown sugar into white. The same white sugar, sucrose, can come from cane or beet.

st.prompt: The English word "sugar" travelled from India through several languages. Which Sanskrit word is it from?

options.t: Sharkara, meaning gravel or grit
Madhu, meaning honey
Mitha, meaning sweet

st.reveal: The crystals reminded people of small grains of gravel, so they were called sharkara. The word passed into Persian and Arabic as shakar and sukkar, then into Latin and English. "Candy" probably comes from khanda, another Indian word for crystal sugar.

myth: Eating sugar makes children hyperactive.

Careful studies, where neither children nor parents knew who had eaten sugar, found no difference in behaviour. Parents who believed their child had eaten sugar were more likely to describe them as hyper. Too much sugar is still bad for teeth and health.

sec.t:
Sugarcane was first farmed in New Guinea, about 8,000 years ago, and spread slowly to South and Southeast Asia. People chewed the canes for their sweet juice.

India was the first place where people learned to boil cane juice and make it into solid sugar that could be stored and traded. Many historians date this to around the Gupta period, about 1,600 years ago, though some say earlier. Indian traders sold it far and wide. The English word sugar comes from the [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] *sharkara*, through Persian and Arabic, and many other languages have similar [[@words-borrowed|borrowed words]].

India still makes plenty of unrefined sugar. [[@jaggery|Jaggery]], or gur, is cane juice boiled in big open pans until it sets into golden or brown blocks. It keeps some of the cane's minerals and molasses, which give it a deep, [[@candy-history|toffee]]-like taste.

Khand is a coarse, partly refined sugar, and mishri is large, clear crystal sugar often offered at temples. In Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra, India's biggest cane-growing states, the crushing season fills villages with the smell of boiling juice.

From the 1500s onwards, European countries set up huge sugar plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean. The work of cutting cane and boiling juice was brutally hard. Millions of Africans were taken by force and enslaved to do it.

After slavery was abolished in the British Empire in the 1830s, plantation owners recruited workers from India on harsh contracts, called indenture. Over the next 80 years, more than a million Indians went to places like Mauritius, Fiji, Trinidad and Guyana, many to work on sugar estates. Their [[descendant|descendants]] form large communities there today.

In 1747, a German chemist named Andreas Marggraf found that beetroots contained the same sugar as cane. The first beet sugar factory opened in 1801 in what is now Poland. Beet sugar meant cool countries could make their own sugar, and today a large share of Europe's sugar comes from beet.

{{story:sugar-teeth}}

Sugar gives quick energy, but [[bacteria|bacteria]] in your mouth love it too. They turn it into [[acid|acid]] that eats into tooth enamel, as you can see in [[@sugar-teeth|why sugar harms teeth]].

The World Health Organization advises that added sugars should make up less than a tenth of the energy a person eats in a day, and ideally less than a twentieth. A single can of a sugary [[@soft-drinks|fizzy drink]] can hold about seven teaspoons of sugar or more. Fruit has natural sugars too, but it comes with fibre and water, which make it far harder to overeat.
